nameStory: The Black Tern gets its name from its striking breeding plumage, when its head, neck, and body turn a deep charcoal-black color that makes it unmistakable among waterbirds. This dramatic seasonal transformation from pale winter colors to bold black summer attire is like watching the bird put on formal evening wear for the breeding season.
description: The Black Tern is a small, graceful waterbird about the size of a robin, with long, pointed wings and a slender build. During breeding season, it sports a distinctive dark charcoal head and body with silvery-gray wings, while in winter it transforms to mostly white with gray patches. Unlike many terns that dive dramatically into the ocean, Black Terns prefer to daintily pick insects and small fish from the surface of freshwater marshes and ponds. They're agile fliers that seem to dance over the water as they hunt.

idTips.label: Breeding Plumage Colors
idTips.description: In summer, the head, neck, and underparts are deep charcoal-black, contrasting sharply with pale gray wings and back - like a bird wearing a black vest over a gray shirt

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with buoyant, erratic wingbeats, often swooping and turning unpredictably as it skims just above the water surface hunting for insects

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Small and compact for a tern, about 9-10 inches long with relatively short, straight black bill and slightly notched tail rather than deeply forked

idTips.label: Feeding Behavior
idTips.description: Picks food delicately from water surface or catches insects in mid-air, rarely diving underwater like ocean terns - more like a swallow than a traditional tern

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Gives sharp 'kek-kek-kek' calls that sound slightly hoarse and metallic, less harsh than the screaming calls of larger terns

idTips.label: Winter Appearance
idTips.description: Transforms to mostly white with gray back and distinctive dark patch behind the eye, making identification much trickier in fall and winter

habitat: Black Terns prefer freshwater marshes, shallow ponds, and wetlands with emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges. In New England, look for them in large marsh systems, flooded meadows, and the shallow edges of lakes and reservoirs, especially those with good populations of aquatic insects. They avoid saltwater habitats and deep, open water, preferring areas where they can easily pick food from the surface.

seasonality.spring: Migrants arrive in late April to May in full breeding plumage, with their striking black heads and bodies making identification straightforward. They begin establishing territories in suitable wetlands and can be seen performing courtship flights.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for observation when birds are nesting and most obvious, actively hunting over marshes with their distinctive black breeding colors. Young birds appear by mid to late summer, looking mottled and brown.
seasonality.fall: Birds begin molting into pale winter plumage by August, making identification much more challenging as they lose their black coloring. Most depart for southern wintering grounds by September.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in New England during winter months, as these birds migrate to tropical coastal areas in South America and Africa. Any tern seen in winter would likely be a different species.

funFact: Black Terns are one of the few tern species that build floating nests, constructing their homes on mats of dead vegetation that rise and fall with changing water levels like tiny rafts - some nests have been found floating freely across ponds while still containing eggs!
confusionNotes: In winter plumage, Black Terns can be confused with other small terns, but look for their compact size and the distinctive dark ear patch. Remember the phrase 'black in breeding, patched in winter' - the dark ear spot is your key winter field mark when the dramatic black plumage is gone.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'tern,' Black Terns behave quite differently from their ocean-going relatives, acting more like flycatchers or swallows as they pick insects from the air and water surface rather than diving for fish. This ecological difference reflects their specialization for inland wetland habitats rather than marine environments.
compareHints: Black Terns are the only marsh terns in New England, making them unique in their genus regionally. Compared to other small terns like Least Terns, Black Terns are darker, chunkier, and prefer freshwater over saltwater habitats. Their surface-feeding behavior and floating nest construction also sets them apart from the diving, ground-nesting habits of most other tern species in the region.
